full_judgment:
6. In resolving the question in controversy, there are inconsistent findings both by the Court of appeal below and the High Court Division. The Courts including the High Court Division are confused in deciding the point in controversy in the light of section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and sections 95 and 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. It is pertinent at this juncture to consider the meaning of the word ''mortgage'' defined in section 58 of the Transfer of the Property Act which means: 

 19. It was argued on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiffs claim of redemption under section 95A of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act being barred, the suit is also barred as being past and closed transaction. This claim was based on a wrong premise. In ''usufructory mortgage'' defined in section 58(d), the mortgagee is placed in possession and has a right to enjoy the usufructs until the debt is paid. As possession by the mortgage is the distinguishing feature of such a mortgage; it follows that there cannot be two different usufructory mortgages on the same property at the same time. When a mortgage was executed and the property mortgaged was leased out to the mortgagee, both formed one transaction which was a usufructory mortgage and not a simple mortgage. The characteristics of a usufructory mortgage are that (a) there is no personal liability on the mortgagor, (b) no time limit is fixed, and (c) the mortgagee takes the whole of the usufructs. 

 29. The case of Ganu Mia vs Abdul labium 10 DLR 636 referred by Mr Bhuiyan was a case under Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1940 and the application was made to the trial Court claiming the transaction as kot mortgage; the deed was executed sometime in 1944. The opposite party resisted the claim stating that the application was not maintainable, inasmuch as, the transaction was an out and out sale and not a mortgage by conditional sale. The trial Court allowed the application holding that the transaction was a mortgage by conditional sale. The appellate Court, however, held that the transaction was an out and out sale with a condition of repurchase and not a mortgage by conditional sale. A Single Bench of the High Court Division on construction of the documents noticed the beginning words ''kabala for absolute sale of immovable property free from encumbrance'' and came to the conclusion that the ''documents themselves seem that these are absolute sale of the land described therein.'' So this case is also quite distinguishable and not applicable in this case. 

 34. The learned Munsif held that the suit as framed is maintainable; that the transaction in question was a mortgage and that the period of limitation is 60 years for redemption of mortgage. The court of appeal below, on the other hand, held that the transaction being out and out sale, the question of redemption of mortgage did not exist; that plaintiffs remedy lay not by way of the suit as framed but by way of appeal against the decision of Debt Settlement Board; and that the suit is barred by limitation. The High Court Division on construction of the impugned deed held that the transaction was a mortgage within the meaning of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 95 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, and not sale with a condition of repurchase. 

 35. The High Court Division unnecessarily took pains by taking into consideration of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act and sections 95 and 95A of the Act of 1950 and arrived at the conclusion that the transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage in view of section 95A of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act incorporated by PO 88 of 1972. It failed to notice that the respondents did not choose the special forum created by the statute. The respondents treated the transaction as one of mortgage by conditional sale and instituted the suit for redemption of mortgage. They did not opt to redeem the mortgage under section 95. The High Court Division was of the view that in view of the words used in second part of section 95A, "or whether transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and the transferee acquires the right to possess, and to enjoy the usufruct of such holding or portion or share thereof for a specified period in lieu of such consideration, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage the relief claimed in the suit would be regulated by section 95A even if the plaintiffs instituted the suit for redemption of mortgage", the law will equally be applicable for redemption of mortgages created at any time. 

 36. There is no recital in the deed that the transferee would enjoy the usufructs of the land for specified period in lieu of the money received by her. It was clearly recited in the deed that the vendors would be entitled to recover the land within a period of five years on repayment of the amount of loan, and in case of failure to repay the said amount, they would be entitled to recover the land through the process of the Court. As observed above, the deed discloses a relationship between the parties as debtor and creditor. The debt subsists and a right to redeem remains with the debtors. The High Court Division failed to consider that after coming into force of Part-V of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act, the Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed. Though Part-V came into force first in Patuakhali on 5th August, 1954 and lastly in Faridpur on 5th August, 1965 by gazette Notifications, laws appended in the schedule to section 80 in their entirety repealed in those areas to the extent mentioned in the fourth column including the Bengal Tenancy Act, so much as those have not been repealed, as for example, the provisions of section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act regarding the right of pre-emption as provided in that section shall apply in its entirety in those areas and not the provisions of section 96 of the Act in respect of cases where application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were filed in courts and during the pendency of those applications, Part-V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in those areas. Thus the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act repealed those previous Tenancy Laws save and except the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 and the Transfer of Property Act, and those unrepealed land laws along with Part V of the Act of 1950 have become the guiding laws of the country. Therefore, those findings are superfious but the ultimate decision of the High Court Division is correct. 

 "It is now submitted before us that in the instant case the parties agreed by the transaction in question that the period of mortgage will be for 5 years beginning from 22-4-1936. So the transaction cannot be said to be alive and subsisting on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No.88 of 1972 i.e. on 3-8-1992. It was past and closed transaction as such the plaintiff cannot claim redemption as the complete usufactory (sic) as contemplated under section 95-A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It has further been submitted that the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division having been made contrary to the decision reported in 1 BLC (AD) 90, 164, 49 DLR (AD) 228 is not sustainable in law inasmuch the impugned judgment is based on misreading of the decisions reported in 32 DLR (AD) 233, 34 DLR (AD) 237 and accordingly is not sustainable in law." 

 52. Since the deed in question is a deed of mortgage, and there cannot be any other mortgage than usufructuary mortgage after 1928 when section 26G was inserted in the Bengal Tenancy Act by Act IV of 1928, it is subject to redemption at the option of the mortgagor within 60 years as provided in article 148 of the Limitation Act, the plaintiffs rightly brought the suit for redemption of the mortgage created by the deed. 

 "5. . . . The maximum period for which a usufructuary mortgage can be entered into was fifteen years under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. But by Ordinance No. XXI of 1969, section 95 was amended and thereby the maximum period for a usufructuary mortgage was reduced to seven years. And unless earlier redeemed by repayment of the consideration a mortgagor acquires right to redemption on the expiry of the maximum period of seven years, and if the mortgage (sic) does not voluntarily restore possession of the land to the mortgagor, the latter may file a suit for redemption within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of his right of redemption. In this case, the suit was filed just on the accrual of the right of redemption and, as such, it is not barred by limitation. 

 "7. The High Court Division relying on the above decision [34 DLR (AD) 237] held that the right of redemption shall accrue after 12 years from 1936, date of mortgage deed and the suit has been filed within a period of 60 years. Accordingly both the courts below committed a gross error of law in construing the President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 and in holding that the mortgage deed was executed in 1936 and section 95 of the State Acquisition of Tenancy Act was amended by promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3-8-1972 and the transaction is a past and closed one, overlooking the vital fact that the mortgagor''s right of redemption within a period of 60 years limitation has not been taken away by president''s Order No. 88 of 1972 rather by promulgating President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 a quick remedy has been made available to a raiyat but it did not in any way affect the long practiced remedy of the right of redemption of mortgage by filing a suit within a period of 60 years from the date of accrual of the right of redemption." 

 "Our conclusions, therefore, are that the President''s Order Nos. 88 and 136 of 1972 and No. 24 of 1973 are all valid legislation for effecting necessary amendments in the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and those laws cannot be attacked on the ground of ultra vires. (2) any transfer of a holding or part thereof by a raiyat either by way of out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey or where the transferor receives from the transferee any consideration and transferee acquires the right to possess and enjoy the usufruct, shall notwithstanding anything contained in the document relating to the transfer, be deemed to be a complete usufructuary mortgage for a period of maximum 7 years and the provisions of section 95(4) and (5) shall apply to such transfers; (3) and such transfers are not to be understood in the light of the Transfer of Property Act because those are to be understood in the light of the enactment in question: (4) those transactions which are subsisting on the date of promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 are hit by section 95A including the transaction entered into by way of an out and out sale with an agreement to reconvey, made whether before or after the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972: and (5) as for the transactions which are not alive before the promulgation of President''s Order No. 88 of 1972 they are concluded by the transactions past and closed."
